title: Critical Ripples and Dirac Fermions in Crystalline Membranes
authors: Sebastián Bahamondes, Rodrigo Soto-Garrido, Enrique Muñoz, Vladimir Juričić
abstract: Crystalline membranes hosting Dirac fermions, with graphene as the paradigmatic example, combine two low-energy sectors with sharply different dynamics: nonrelativistic flexural phonons and relativistic-like Dirac quasiparticles. We develop the low-energy field theory of this coupled system at charge neutrality and determine how this dynamical mismatch controls the coupling between the two sectors. In the long-wavelength flat phase, rotational symmetry ties the renormalization of the leading local scalar strain--density coupling to the scale-dependent bending rigidity, causing its dimensionless strength to decrease logarithmically. At the same time, flexural modes become parametrically slower than the Dirac fermions, so the resulting fermionic feedback vanishes as a power law.The flat phase is therefore stable against this perturbation. The physics changes when elastic interactions or electronic softening destabilize the membrane at a finite wavelength, selecting a ripple pattern formed by modes at $\pm\mathbf{Q}$. For an isolated pair of ordering wavevectors, provided that commensurability-induced phase pinning is irrelevant, the transition is governed by the bosonic Wilson--Fisher fixed point, while the Dirac fermions remain spectators. A genuinely hybrid electronic--structural critical point arises instead when symmetry permits a mass-type Dirac bilinear to share the ripple's momentum and quantum numbers, including horizontal-reflection parity. The transition is then described by the chiral-XY Gross--Neveu--Yukawa universality class. Using the known one-loop critical exponents, we characterize this transition, determine the induced secondary elastic distortion, and show that the fermionic and bosonic velocities lock in the isotropic continuum limit.
summary: This theoretical work develops a field theory for crystalline membranes coupling flexural phonons with Dirac fermions. Using Renormalization Group techniques, the authors determine that while the system can remain stable in the flat limit, instabilities at finite wavelengths lead to distinct critical points. The most complex case involves a hybrid transition characterized by the chiral-XY Gross-Neveu-Yukawa universality class.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the low-energy field theory describing the coupled dynamics between nonrelativistic flexural phonons and relativistic Dirac quasiparticles in crystalline membranes.
main_result: It distinguishes two critical scenarios: a stable flat phase, or genuine hybrid electronic-structural critical points governed by the chiral-XY Gross-Neveu-Yukawa universality class when symmetry permits coupling.
method: The analysis relies heavily on Renormalization Group (RG) flow techniques and one-loop calculations to determine the stability of different physical regimes and characterize critical exponents.
model_or_system: The system is a crystalline membrane hosting Dirac fermions, modeled by coupled effective actions for flexural phonons and massless Dirac quasiparticles. The coupling strength and renormalization are key focus areas.
key_observables: Critical exponents (e.g., related to Wilson-Fisher or chiral-XY classes), renormalized elastic constants, and the flow of dimensionless coupling strengths ($ ar{g}, y$).
important_parameters: The ratio between flexural and Dirac energy scales ($s(\ell)$), charge neutrality conditions, and symmetry constraints (e.g., horizontal reflection parity).
main_assumptions: The analysis separates the infrared behavior (flat phase) from potential instabilities at finite momentum ($\pm Q$), and assumes specific symmetries dictate which universality class applies.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the structure implies showing RG flow diagrams or critical exponents for different coupling regimes.
paper_structure: The paper develops the coupled low-energy field theory, analyzes the stability of the long-wavelength flat phase via RG flow, and then examines two distinct instability scenarios: one governed by bosonic Wilson-Fisher fixed points, and a second, hybrid case leading to chiral-XY GNY universality.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of critical phenomena concepts (RG theory) to coupled electronic/structural degrees of freedom is highly relevant for understanding quantum phase transitions in low-dimensional materials that bridge solid-state physics and statistical mechanics.

Panels (a) and (b) generate the pure-membrane renormalizations in eqs. (3.1)–(3.3). Panel (c) is the isotropic-tension insertion entering eqs. (3.6) and (3.16); its Ward-identity derivation is given in appendices B and D. Panel (d) generates the nonlocal strain interaction in eq. (3.28), with the polarization given in eq. (3.26).

Figure 2. Finite-momentum couplings. Solid directed lines denote Dirac propagators and dashed lines denote bosonic fields. Each arrow is centered on its uninterrupted propagator segment; open fermion lines are oriented from left to right. Panel (a) represents the mechanical density interaction in eq. (4.7). Panel (b) is the symmetry-locked Yukawa vertex in eq. (5.1). Panel (c) depicts the bilinear electronic–structural mixing in eq. (5.6), which induces the relation in eq. (5.7).

Figure 3. One-loop diagrams of the finite-Q GNY theory. Solid lines denote Dirac propagators and dashed lines denote bosonic order-parameter propagators. Arrows are centered on the internal fermion segments between vertices; open fermion lines are oriented from left to right, while arrows on closed loops follow a consistent circulation. Panels (a) and (b) determine the anomalous dimensions in eqs. (5.16) and (5.17); panels (c) and (d) contribute to the beta functions in eqs. (5.10) and (5.11). The pole parts and normalization conventions are collected in appendix F.
